title: With Due Respect (Vol. 2) -- Ch. 10: Contempt and Disciplinary Actions
keywords: a rash act of misplaced vigilance
Re: Letter of the UP Law Faculty
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2) -- CJP's November 7, 2010 Inquirer column explaining how the Supreme Court could, even without any complainant, conduct contempt and disciplinary proceedings against 37 UP law professors for a public 'Statement' on a pending case

The source and basis: the professors' statement urging Justice Del Castillo's resignation over plagiarism allegations led the Court to order them to show cause under the Code of Professional Responsibility (Canons 10, 11, 13), with Dean Marvic Leonen separately cited for submitting a 'dummy... not a true and faithful reproduction' of the statement

Why the Court felt aggrieved: it deemed the faculty's denunciation of its Vinuya v. Executive Secretary ruling (which dismissed the comfort women's petition) a 'rash act of misplaced vigilance' that, with the Vinuya reconsideration still pending, risked 'tending to influence the decision' -- itself contempt

The distinction between 'inquisitorial' contempt/disciplinary proceedings (where 'the judge is the offended party, plaintiff, and prosecutor' at once) and ordinary 'adversarial' litigation -- and the 'greatness and humility' the Court would need to balance its dignity against the professors' free expression, 'answerable to history'
sub_topics: The readers' puzzle: why could the Court, 'even without a complaint from anyone,' move against 37 UP law professors for 'merely expressing their opinion on a court decision'?

The trigger and charges: the professors' 'Statement' calling 'for the resignation of Justice Mariano C. Del Castillo' amid plagiarism allegations led the Court to require them to show cause for possible violations of Canons 10, 11 and 13 and Rules 1.02 and 11.05 of the Code of Professional Responsibility, which bar lawyers from any impropriety 'which tends to influence or gives the appearance of influencing the court'

Dean Leonen singled out: directed to show cause under Canon 10 (Rules 10.01-10.03) for submitting 'a dummy which is not a true and faithful reproduction' of the statement, the canons forbidding lawyers to 'do any falsehood'

The Court's grievance: it felt the faculty had branded its Vinuya v. Executive Secretary decision (April 28, 2010, dismissing several comfort women's petition) 'a reprehensible act of dishonesty and misrepresentation,' aggravated by imputations of deliberate delay, reliance on 'polluted sources,' and indifference

The contempt rationale: because the Vinuya 'motion for reconsideration... is still pending,' the Court called the condemnation 'totally unnecessary, uncalled for and a rash act of misplaced vigilance,' warning that publication 'tending to influence the decision of the controversy is contempt of court and is punishable'

Separate and extraordinary: the show-cause matter was docketed as a 'regular administrative matter' apart from Vinuya, titled 'Re: Letter of the UP Law Faculty' with 'no plaintiff or petitioner, only respondents' -- the Court itself initiating, investigating and deciding, while affording due-process chance to explain

Inquisitorial vs. adversarial: in adversarial litigation courts are 'very passive' and Edmund Burke's 'cold neutrality of an impartial judge' is obvious; in inquisitorial contempt and disciplinary cases, 'the judge is the offended party, plaintiff, and prosecutor at the same time,' putting that 'cold neutrality' at issue

Greatness and humility: the Court must 'carefully balance the need to uphold its dignity and honor' against 'the professors' right to free expression,' as 'both the offended party and the judge' answerable to no higher court but 'answerable to history' -- and it 'takes great humility to reverse or modify their earlier strong opinion' in the show-cause resolution; a footnote notes the inquisitorial method has always governed judge-initiated contempt since the Court's 1901 founding

stances.claim: The Court could move against the 37 professors without any complainant because contempt and disciplinary proceedings are 'inquisitorial,' not 'adversarial': the Court itself initiates, investigates and decides, docketing the matter as 'Re: Letter of the UP Law Faculty' with no plaintiff, only respondents -- while still affording them due process to explain.

stances.claim: The Court felt entitled to act because the faculty's statement -- calling its Vinuya ruling 'a reprehensible act of dishonesty' while the reconsideration was 'still pending' -- was 'a rash act of misplaced vigilance,' and publication 'tending to influence' a pending decision 'is contempt of court and is punishable.'

stances.claim: In such inquisitorial proceedings 'the judge is the offended party, plaintiff, and prosecutor at the same time,' so the Court must balance its 'dignity and honor' against 'the professors' right to free expression' with 'great humility' -- willing to 'reverse or modify' its strong show-cause resolution, knowing it is 'answerable to history.'

notable_anecdotes: Action without a complainant: CJP opens with readers' bewilderment that the Court could discipline 37 UP professors 'even without a complaint from anyone' for voicing an opinion on a decision.

The 'dummy' against Dean Leonen: he notes Dean Marvic Leonen was singled out for submitting 'a dummy which is not a true and faithful reproduction' of the faculty statement, drawing a separate show-cause order on falsehood.

Judge as offended party: he crystallizes the unease by observing that in inquisitorial contempt, 'the judge is the offended party, plaintiff, and prosecutor at the same time,' straining Burke's 'cold neutrality of an impartial judge.'

Humility from Scripture: he closes that 'it takes great humility to reverse or modify' the show-cause resolution, recalling that 'the greatest in the kingdom,' Jesus said, 'are also the humblest,' and footnotes that judge-initiated contempt has always been decided inquisitorially since 1901.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 2), CJP's November 7, 2010 Inquirer column, explains how the Supreme Court could, 'even without a complaint from anyone,' pursue contempt and disciplinary action against 37 University of the Philippines law professors for a public statement on a pending case. The 'Statement' had called 'for the resignation of Justice Mariano C. Del Castillo' over plagiarism allegations, leading the Court to order the faculty to show cause under Canons 10, 11 and 13 of the Code of Professional Responsibility -- which bar lawyers from impropriety 'which tends to influence... the court' -- with Dean Marvic Leonen separately cited under Canon 10 for submitting 'a dummy which is not a true and faithful reproduction' of the statement. The Court felt aggrieved that the professors branded its Vinuya v. Executive Secretary ruling (April 28, 2010, dismissing several comfort women's petition) 'a reprehensible act of dishonesty and misrepresentation,' and, because the Vinuya reconsideration was 'still pending,' deemed the condemnation 'a rash act of misplaced vigilance,' warning that publication 'tending to influence the decision... is contempt of court and is punishable.' CJP then demystifies the proceeding: docketed as a 'regular administrative matter' titled 'Re: Letter of the UP Law Faculty,' it has 'no plaintiff or petitioner, only respondents,' because such contempt and disciplinary cases are 'inquisitorial' rather than 'adversarial' -- the Court itself initiating, investigating and deciding (while still granting due-process chance to explain), unlike ordinary litigation where courts stay 'passive' and Burke's 'cold neutrality of an impartial judge' is plain. The tension, he stresses, is that in inquisitorial contempt 'the judge is the offended party, plaintiff, and prosecutor at the same time,' so the Court must balance 'its dignity and honor' against 'the professors' right to free expression' with 'great humility' -- ready to 'reverse or modify' its strong show-cause resolution, for though no higher court can review it, it remains 'answerable to history,' and 'the greatest in the kingdom... are also the humblest.'
